message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"10.11","text":"For, knowing the law from the beginning—that if he merely brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods, so that you sin against the good of sole rule, your destruction becomes gain for him (and this is because, having been condemned to eat earth, he has authority to eat the person who through sin has dissolved into earth and become earth, while your souls pass into the belly of his fire)—he therefore, so that you may suffer these things, suggests to you every notion directed against you.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς νόμον","chosen":"the law from the beginning","rationale":"Preserves the temporal phrase; “the original law” is possible but would make its characterization less explicit."},{"source_quote":"εἰς ὑπόνοιαν ὡνδήποτε λεγομένων θεῶν ἐνέγκῃ","chosen":"brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods","rationale":"ὑπόνοια denotes a notion or supposition here, while λεγομένων marks them as beings designated or said to be gods."},{"source_quote":"τὸ τῆς μοναρχίας ἀγαθὸν","chosen":"the good of sole rule","rationale":"μοναρχία refers contextually to the rule of one God; “sole rule” preserves that claim without importing a familiar theological formula."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὴν τοῦ πυρὸς αὐτοῦ γαστέρα","chosen":"into the belly of his fire","rationale":"Retains the source’s unusual image and possessive attachment rather than replacing it with the smoother “fiery belly.”"},{"source_quote":"πᾶσαν τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν ὑμῖν ὑποβάλλει οἴησιν","chosen":"suggests to you every notion directed against you","rationale":"καθ’ ὑμῶν describes the notions as working against their recipients; οἴησις may also be rendered “opinion” or “supposition.”"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"10.12","text":"For all the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule are sown by him into your mind for your harm. First, so that after hearing the words concerning reverence for God you may not drive away ignorance, the cause of evils, he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge. At first he uses one preconception applied to everyone: the idea that one has decided wisely because, if someone does not hear the message concerning reverence for God, he is not “liable to judgment.” Therefore some, deceived in this way, do not wish to listen, so that they may remain ignorant, not knowing that ignorance is itself, on its own, enough of a deadly poison. For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die. In the same way, sins by their nature destroy the sinner, even if in ignorance he does what he ought not to do.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"αἱ κατὰ τῆς μοναρχίας ἀπατηλοὶ ... ὑπολήψεις","chosen":"the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule","rationale":"ὑπολήψεις are received notions or suppositions, and κατὰ marks their opposition to divine sole rule."},{"source_quote":"προφάσει γνώσεως ἐνεδρεύει ψευδοῦς","chosen":"he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge","rationale":"ψευδοῦς grammatically modifies γνώσεως; “under the pretext” conveys the instrumental dative προφάσει."},{"source_quote":"μιᾷ τῇ κατὰ πάντων προλήψει","chosen":"one preconception applied to everyone","rationale":"κατὰ πάντων may mean universal application or direction against everyone; the rendering preserves the universal scope in this context."},{"source_quote":"τὸ νομίζειν καλῶς βεβουλεῦσθαι ὅτι","chosen":"the idea that one has decided wisely because","rationale":"The middle perfect βεβουλεῦσθαι can describe having formed a supposedly wise resolution; alternatively, the phrase may be understood impersonally as “thinking it has been wisely determined that.”"},{"source_quote":"οὐ γάρ, εἴ τις προσλάβοι θανασίμου φαρμάκου ἀγνοῶν, οὐκ ἀποθνήσκει","chosen":"For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die","rationale":"The expanded English preserves the emphatic Greek double negative and the analogy between unknown poison and unwitting sin."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"αἱ ἁμαρτία ἀναιροῦσιν","issue":"The singular-looking form ἁμαρτία conflicts with both the plural article αἱ and the plural verb ἀναιροῦσιν. The context clearly requires a plural subject, so the printed form appears to lack the final ι of the nominative plural.","proposed_reading":"αἱ ἁμαρτίαι ἀναιροῦσιν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"10.13","text":"But if judgment comes on account of disobedience to words, much more will God destroy those who have refused to accept the worship directed toward him. For the one who does not wish to learn, lest he be liable, is already judged as one who knows. For the one who does not wish to listen has understood; thus no contrivance can serve as a defense before God, the “knower of hearts.” Therefore flee the crafty thought that the serpent insinuates into your mind. Even if, then, someone truly ends the present life in ignorance, he will face the charge that, though he lived for a time, he did not know who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him, and that, as an insensible and ungrateful, very unworthy servant, he is rejected from the kingdom of God.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ παρακοῇ λόγων","chosen":"on account of disobedience to words","rationale":"παρακοή can denote either failure to hear or disobedience; the context concerns culpable refusal to listen, and “disobedience” preserves that moral force."},{"source_quote":"τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν θρησκείαν ἀναδέξασθαι","chosen":"to accept the worship directed toward him","rationale":"θρησκεία denotes religious observance or worship, while εἰς αὐτόν explicitly supplies its direction."},{"source_quote":"ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει","chosen":"For the one who does not wish to listen has understood","rationale":"The aorist ἔγνω is retained as an assertion of culpable awareness. “Has come to know” is also possible, but the context treats refusal itself as evidence of knowledge."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς „καρδιογνώστην“ θεόν","chosen":"before God, the “knower of hearts”","rationale":"The rendering retains the source’s quotation marks around the descriptive compound καρδιογνώστης."},{"source_quote":"ἵνα δὲ καὶ ὄντως ἀγνοήσας τις τὸν παρόντα βίον τελευτήσει","chosen":"Even if, then, someone truly ends the present life in ignorance","rationale":"ἵνα with the future indicative is understood concessively or hypothetically in context; a more formally literal “suppose that” would express the same argumentative concession."},{"source_quote":"τίς αὐτῷ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτῷ ἐπιχορηγηθεισῶν τροφῶν ὑπῆρξεν εὐεργέτης","chosen":"who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him","rationale":"The Greek coordinates the personal beneficiary and the supplied provisions somewhat unevenly. “Source” conveys the beneficent provision without inventing a second actor."},{"source_quote":"δοῦλος","chosen":"servant","rationale":"The policy-default rendering is used; the term still presents the person as belonging to and accountable to a superior."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"10.14","text":"Again, the formidable serpent suggests to you that you should think this and say this very thing, which nearly all of you say: “We too know that the Lord of all is one, but these also are gods. For just as Caesar is one but has administrators under him—consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten—in the same way, since the great God is one, like Caesar, they too are gods by analogy with the subordinate authorities: they are subject to him but administer us.” Listen, then, you who have been smeared by him with this supposition as with a terrible poison—I mean the evil implication of the example—so that you may know what is good and what is evil. For you have not yet regained your sight, since you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὁ δεινὸς ὄφις","chosen":"the formidable serpent","rationale":"δεινός can mean formidable, terrible, or fearsome; “formidable” fits the serpent’s dangerous cunning without weakening the description."},{"source_quote":"ὑπατικούς, ἐπάρχους, χιλιάρχους, ἑκατοντάρχους, δεκαδάρχους","chosen":"consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten","rationale":"The transparent numerical renderings preserve the descending administrative or military hierarchy; ὑπατικοί denotes persons of consular standing rather than ordinary consuls."},{"source_quote":"κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐξουσιῶν λόγον","chosen":"by analogy with the subordinate authorities","rationale":"λόγος here expresses the proposed correspondence or analogy, though “according to the status of the subordinate authorities” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ὡς δεινῷ ὑπαλειφθέντες ἰῷ","chosen":"smeared ... as with a terrible poison","rationale":"Retains the physical image of ὑπαλείφω, “smear” or “anoint,” and the comparison of the supposition to poison."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ παραδείγματος τὴν κακὴν ὑπόνοιαν","chosen":"the evil implication of the example","rationale":"Here ὑπόνοια is the underlying implication carried by the Caesar analogy, rather than merely a suspicion."},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ τοῖς προβαλλομένοις ὑφ’ ὑμῶν ἐνορᾶτε","chosen":"you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward","rationale":"The wording preserves the distinction between advancing an argument and discerning what lies within or follows from it."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὕπω γὰρ ἀνεβλέψατε","issue":"The printed οὕπω has a rough breathing and circumflex-like spelling where the negative adverb meaning “not yet” is conventionally written οὔπω. The context unambiguously requires the negative sense.","proposed_reading":"οὔπω γὰρ ἀνεβλέψατε","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"10.15","text":"For if you say that God, on the analogy of Caesar, has subordinate authorities—the beings called gods—even so you do not follow your own example. For if you did follow it, you ought to know this: just as it is not permissible to give Caesar’s name to another—I mean, to a consul, a prefect, a commander of a thousand, or anyone else—because the giver will not live and the receiver will be put to death, so, by your own example, it is not permissible for the name “God” to be given to another, since even the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it perishes. And if an affront in a human case incurs punishment, much more will those who call others gods, as people who have insulted God, be subject to eternal punishment. And rightly so, because you have subjected the name entrusted to you for honoring his sole rule to every insult of which you were capable. For “God” is not his true name. Rather, you received for the present what was given to you and insulted it, so that whatever use you made of it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name; but you subjected it to every insult.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν τοῦ Καίσαρος λόγον","chosen":"on the analogy of Caesar","rationale":"λόγος refers to the proposed correspondence between divine and imperial administration; “according to Caesar’s model” is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὸ Καίσαρος ὄνομα","chosen":"Caesar’s name","rationale":"ὄνομα may also mean title or designation here, but “name” is retained because the passage explicitly compares it with the name “God.”"},{"source_quote":"ὁ πεισθεὶς εἴτε λαβεῖν εἴτε δοῦναι","chosen":"the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it","rationale":"The passive participle is preserved; the unnamed object is contextually the disputed name or designation."},{"source_quote":"ἡ ἀπ’ ἀνθρώπου ὕβρις","chosen":"an affront in a human case","rationale":"The ἀπό phrase is compact and may describe an insult involving a human being, an insult committed by one, or punishment at human hands. The contextual rendering leaves the precise direction open while preserving the human-versus-divine comparison."},{"source_quote":"τὸ εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν παραδοθὲν ὑμῖν τιμᾶν ὄνομα","chosen":"the name entrusted to you for honoring his sole rule","rationale":"The infinitive τιμᾶν expresses the purpose for which the name was entrusted, while εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν identifies the honor as directed toward God’s sole rule."},{"source_quote":"οὐ γὰρ τὸ ὄντως ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ ὄνομα θεός","chosen":"For “God” is not his true name","rationale":"The clause distinguishes the designation θεός from God’s actual or true name; quotation marks clarify that the word itself is under discussion."},{"source_quote":"τέως παρειληφότες","chosen":"received for the present","rationale":"τέως may mean “for the present” or “up to now.” The former suits the contrast between the received designation and the true name, while the temporal alternative remains possible."},{"source_quote":"ἵνα ὡς ἂν αὐτῷ χρήσῃσθε, εἰς τὸ ὄντως αὐτοῦ ὄνομα λογισθῇ","chosen":"so that whatever use you made of it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name","rationale":"The subject of λογισθῇ is implicit in Greek and is understood as the use or treatment of the received designation; more literally, it might be “might be reckoned toward his true name.”"}],"source_issues":[]}]}
